**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Persist sync outcomes for waitForUpload callers**

`waitForUpload` only registers a new listener and never checks whether that upload session has already completed, so completion can be lost if `notifyListeners` ran earlier with no listeners attached. In the offline client flow, `done()` waits for staging before calling `waitForUpload`, so a quick reconnect/sync can finish first and the later `done()` call will hang forever because no future notification is emitted for that session.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Trigger initial sync when auto-sync starts online**

`startAutoSync()` only subscribes to future `online` events and never runs `syncAll()` immediately when the app is already online. That leaves previously staged uploads (for example, from an earlier offline session or tab restart) unsynced indefinitely until connectivity toggles again or someone manually calls sync, which violates expected auto-sync behavior.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Handle empty successful responses in request helper**

The shared `request` helper unconditionally executes `response.json()` for every successful response. Endpoints like `deleteFile` commonly return `204 No Content`, and parsing JSON on an empty body throws, turning a successful delete into a client error (and potentially triggering unnecessary retries).

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**`waitForUpload` can hang forever if sync races ahead of the listener** `done()` first awaits `stagePromise` (completing the OPFS write), then calls `waitForUpload` to register a listener. But `startAutoSync()` subscribes to the browser `online` event and calls `syncAll()` immediately. If connectivity is restored after staging completes but before `done()` reaches `waitForUpload`, the following race occurs: 1. `stagePromise` resolves → upload is in OPFS. 2. `online` fires → `syncAll()` runs → finds the session → calls `notifyListeners(uploadSessionId, result)` → **no listener registered yet** → notification is silently discarded. 3. `done()` resumes → calls `waitForUpload(uploadSessionId)` → registers a listener that will **never be called** → `done()` hangs indefinitely. The fix is to either keep a `completedResults` map in `OfflineSync` so `waitForUpload` can return immediately if the result is already available, or have `waitForUpload` check the store for the session after registering its listener.

🌐 Web query:

`Fetch API Response.json() empty body 204 No Content behavior`

💡 Result:

With the Fetch API, an HTTP **204 No Content** response **must not include a message body**, and HTTP clients should treat it as body-less. In HTTP/1.1, such responses are terminated right after the headers (first empty line). [1]

Because of that, calling **`response.json()`** on a 204 response typically **rejects** (e.g., `SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input`), since there are **zero bytes** to parse as JSON. This has long been observed/raised in Fetch implementations/spec discussion. [2][3]

### Practical handling pattern
```js
const res = await fetch(url);

if (res.status === 204) return null;          // or {} or whatever your app expects

// optionally also guard on content-type
// if (res.headers.get("content-type")?.includes("application/json") !== true) ...

return await res.json();
```

If you *want* to always call `.json()` successfully, don’t return 204—return **200** with a valid JSON body like `{}` or `[]` instead. [4]

**Sources:**  
[1] RFC 9112 (HTTP/1.1) statement that 204 responses have no message body and end after headers https://www.hjp.at/%28de%29/doc/rfc/rfc9112.pdf  
[2] WHATWG Fetch issue: `response.json()` on 204 throws “unexpected end of input” https://github.com/whatwg/fetch/issues/113  
[3] MDN: `Response.json()` reads the body stream and throws if it can’t be parsed as JSON https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Response/json  
[4] Postman: 204 indicates success with intentionally no response body (use 200 if you need a body) https://blog.postman.com/http-204-no-content/

🌐 Web query:

`Fetch API Response body single-consumption stream double read error`

💡 Result:

In `fetch()`, the `Response` body is a **single-consumption stream**. Once you read it with `response.json()`, `response.text()`, `response.blob()`, etc., `bodyUsed` becomes true and any later attempt to read it again throws errors like **“body stream already read”**. [1][2]

**Fix options:**

1) **Read once, reuse the parsed value**
```js
const res = await fetch(url);
const data = await res.json();   // read once
// use `data` everywhere; don’t call res.json()/res.text() again
```

2) **Clone before reading twice (e.g., log raw text + parse JSON)**
```js
const res = await fetch(url);
const res2 = res.clone();        // must be BEFORE first read [1][2]

const raw = await res2.text();
const data = await res.json();
```
`Response.clone()` exists specifically to allow multiple reads of an otherwise one-use body, and it throws if the body was already used. [1][2]

3) **If you’re consuming as a stream (`response.body`)**
Use stream teeing (`ReadableStream.tee()`) or create separate consumers; don’t attach multiple readers to the same stream. (The underlying body is a `ReadableStream`.) [3]

**Debug tip:** check `response.bodyUsed` before/after a read to confirm what consumed it. [2]

Sources:  
[1] MDN: `Response.clone()` throws if body already used; enables multiple uses of one-use bodies. ([developer.mozilla.org](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Response/clone?utm_source=openai))  
[2] Mozilla Hacks: Request/Response bodies can only be read once; clone must be called before use. ([hacks.mozilla.org](https://hacks.mozilla.org/2015/03/this-api-is-so-fetching/?utm_source=openai))  
[3] MDN “Using the Fetch API”: response bodies are streams; reading methods consume the body. ([developer.mozilla.org](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Fetch_API/Using_Fetch...?utm_source=openai))

Citations:

- 1: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Response/clone?utm_source=openai
- 2: https://hacks.mozilla.org/2015/03/this-api-is-so-fetching/?utm_source=openai

`response.json()` rejects on a standard `204 No Content` response, which breaks `deleteFile()` since DELETE operations typically return empty bodies. The error handling path compounds this by attempting to read the response body twice—first with `response.json()`, then falling back to `response.text()`—but since the Fetch API Response body is a single-consumption stream, the second read throws "body stream already read" and masks the original HTTP error.
